title: Nvidia paper finds AI models lose accuracy on long tasks, with steep drops at scale
key_facts: Nvidia researchers released a paper on 30 Sep 2026, 'Staying on Task: Testing the Foundations of Long-Horizon Agent Reliability' (arXiv:2609.38712), introducing a benchmark called Long-Transduction.
The tests were deliberately simple (arithmetic, sorting UUIDs, looking up variables, transforming tables) and checked whether models keep track of state over long input.
Seven open-weight models (models whose trained settings are public) were run on 1,440 documents each, with input growing from 4,000 to 128,000 tokens, scored by exact match.
Average accuracy fell by 62.8% from 4K to 128K tokens.
DeepSeek's score went from 0.909 to 0.554; Nvidia's own Nemotron Super fell from 0.711 to 0.138.
Missing item identifiers and greater local complexity also hurt, and the paper says these weaknesses compound.
The authors advise splitting long tasks into smaller subtasks and labelling each item with a structured identifier.
The article says this adds to a growing body of 2025 and 2026 research on long-horizon limits.
quote_evidence: In a paper released on September 30, 2026, Nvidia researchers found that average model accuracy fell by 62.8% as context length scaled up.
DeepSeek started strong, scoring 0.909 at the shorter length.
Nvidia’s own Nemotron Super fared worse. It fell from 0.711 to 0.138.
why_it_matters_hint: A model that accepts very long text may not reliably work through it, which matters for AI agents given long jobs.
notes: Secondary coverage of an arXiv preprint; the paper itself was not read and no outside review is reported. The paper is dated 30 Sep 2026, before 2 Oct, so score lowered 6 to 5. Only seven open models and simple tasks were tested.
